hook.ref: Mahabharata · Udyoga Parva · Udyoga: Krishna's peace embassy
hook.speaker: Yudhishthira
hook.setting: Before Krishna leaves for the Kaurava court, Yudhishthira lays out why he wants peace, not war.
hook.sanskrit: अधनाद्धि निवर्तन्ते ज्ञातयः सुहृदो द्विजाः / अपुष्पादफलाद्वृक्षाद्यथा कृष्ण पतत्रिणः
hook.line: When money runs out, some friends drift away, like birds leaving a tree with no fruit.
hook.translation: When a man has no money, relatives, friends and brahmins turn away from him, the way birds leave a tree that has no flowers and no fruit.
hook.why: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

prasang.title: Yudhishthira's case for peace
prasang.summary: Before Krishna sets out as peace envoy, Yudhishthira opens his heart: poverty humiliates, greed corrodes, victory breeds enmity, and hostility is never ended by hostility. He asks only for five villages.
prasang.lesson: Winning a feud still costs you peace. Hostility only ends when someone stops feeding it.

hook.for_you: You feel on your own with this, and a verse has been chosen with it in mind.
hook.first_line: You feel on your own with this, and a verse has been chosen with it in mind.

alternates.speaker: Vibhishan
alternates.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
alternates.sanskrit: सुनहु पवनसुत रहनि हमारी। जिमि दसनन्हि महुँ जीभ बिचारी॥ तात कबहुँ मोहि जानि अनाथा। करिहहिं कृपा भानुकुल नाथा ॥
alternates.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
alternates.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?
alternates.why: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

prasang.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
prasang.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
prasang.story_hook: In a city of demons, Hanuman heard someone wake up and say Ram's name.
prasang.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

alternates.speaker: Tulsidas
alternates.setting: Tulsidas on his own childhood: abandoned at birth, he grew up begging.
alternates.sanskrit: मातु-पिताँ जग जाइ तज्यो बिधिहूँ न लिखी कछु भाल भलाई। नीच, निरादरभाजन, कादर, कूकर-टूकन लागि ललाई॥ रामु-सुभाउ सुन्यो तुलसीं प्रभुसों कह्यो बारक पेटु खलाई। स्वारथको परमारथको रघुनाथु सो साहेबु, खोरि न लाई॥
alternates.line: Abandoned as a child, he poured out his hunger just once, and was held.
alternates.translation: My mother and father brought me into the world and left me; fate wrote nothing good on my forehead. Lowly, scorned, timid, I hungered like a dog for scraps. Then Tulsi heard of Ram's nature and, just once, showed the Lord his empty stomach. Such a master is Raghunath that he held nothing back, in this world or the next.

verse.for_you: The ones who remain are the ones who value you. Their quiet presence is enough.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today where you are still whole, without needing an audience to prove it.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the flat, and the quiet remains, as Yudhishthira sat with the weight of loss and the cost of friendship.

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
verse.line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.
verse.translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.
verse.why: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

prasang.title: Ridicule, opposition, acceptance (letter to Khetri, 1895)
prasang.summary: Facing opposition from some clergy in America, he writes to his friend the Maharaja that every work passes through ridicule, opposition and then acceptance. Anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood, so he will stay steady.
prasang.lesson: Ridicule and opposition are stages, not verdicts.

why: being mocked and opposed for one's work

verse.speaker: Sugriva
verse.setting: Newly bound in friendship, Sugriva tells Ram what a friend means to him.
verse.sanskrit: आढ्यो वापि दरिद्रो वा दुःखितः सुखितोऽपि वा। निर्दोषश्च सदोषश्च वयस्यः परमा गतिः॥
verse.line: Rich or poor, happy or sad, flawed or not, a friend is your greatest refuge.
verse.translation: Rich or poor, happy or unhappy, faultless or flawed, a friend is one's greatest refuge.
verse.why: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

prasang.title: Ram and Sugriva's friendship
prasang.summary: Ram and Sugriva swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva shows Ram the jewels Sita dropped; Ram breaks down, and Sugriva comforts him: in trouble the steady person thinks it through, and a friend is the greatest refuge.
prasang.story_hook: Two exiles, each robbed of his wife and home, swore friendship over a fire.
prasang.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

verse.for_you: You stand at the edge of a quiet flat, the absence of twelve years sitting beside you. A friend is your greatest refuge, and you are already in one.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing today that reminds you you are still here, with yourself.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet flat, and the memory of twelve years stands with you.

why: Find the friend; trees that stand together hold each other up.
a friend is named as refuge in every condition

verse.speaker: Vidura
verse.setting: Vidura counsels the sleepless King Dhritarashtra the night before the peace talks.
verse.sanskrit: महानप्येकजो वृक्षो बलवान्सुप्रतिष्ठितः / प्रसह्य एव वातेन सस्कन्धो मर्दितुं क्षणात् अथ ये सहिता वृक्षाः सङ्घशः सुप्रतिष्ठिताः / ते हि शीघ्रतमान्वातान्सहन्तेन्योन्यसंश्रयात्
verse.line: A lone tree falls to the storm; trees that stand together hold each other up.
verse.translation: A single tree, however great, strong and deep-rooted, can be wrenched out trunk and all by the wind in a moment. But trees that stand together, rooted in a cluster, withstand the fiercest winds by leaning on one another.
verse.why: When insulted, don't insult back. Swallow anger, and stand with your own people.

prasang.title: Vidura Niti: Atreya and the Sadhyas, on insult and anger
prasang.summary: Vidura retells the sage Atreya's answer to the gods: don't insult back, hold your tongue, choose your company. He adds that anger is a bitter drink and that kin who stand together survive storms.
prasang.lesson: When insulted, don't insult back. Swallow anger, and stand with your own people.

why: Find the friend; trees that stand together hold each other up.
Standing alone is the risk; leaning on others is strength

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Arjuna asks which devotee is best; Krishna offers a ladder of practices.
verse.sanskrit: अभ्यासेऽप्यसमर्थोऽसि मत्कर्मपरमो भव । मदर्थमपि कर्माणि कुर्वन् सिद्धिमवाप्स्यसि ॥
verse.line: If even practice is too hard, just do your work for my sake. That alone takes you far.
verse.translation: If you are unable even to practise, be intent on doing work for my sake. Even by doing actions for me, you will reach perfection.
verse.why: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

prasang.title: Form or formless: which devotee is best, and the ways to reach him
prasang.summary: Krishna says devotion to a personal form is easier, then offers a ladder: fix your mind; if not, practise; if not, work for me; if not, let go of results. Letting go brings peace at once.
prasang.lesson: If the ideal is too hard, take the next step down, and keep going.

why: dedicating ordinary work to him
work done for his sake

verse.speaker: Vibhishana
verse.setting: Insulted for urging peace, Vibhishana leaves his brother's court for good.
verse.sanskrit: तन्मर्षयतु यच्चोक्तं गुरुत्वाद्धितमिच्छता। आत्मानं सर्वथा रक्ष पुरीं चेमां सराक्षसाम्। स्वस्ति तेऽस्तु गमिष्यामि सुखी भव मया विना॥
verse.line: I said it for your good. I wish you well. I'm leaving. Be happy without me.
verse.translation: Forgive what I said; I said it for your good, out of respect for you as my elder. Protect yourself and this city. I wish you well. I am leaving. Be happy without me.
verse.why: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.
verse.misuse: Walking away from family is a last resort after honest counsel fails, not a first response to disagreement.

prasang.title: Vibhishana tells his brother the truth
prasang.summary: In Ravana's war council, everyone else flatters him. Vibhishana alone says what he has seen: return Sita, avoid war. Ravana insults him as a traitor. Vibhishana says flatterers are easy to find and truth-tellers rare, wishes his brother well, and leaves.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone in the hall agreed with the king, except his youngest brother.
prasang.lesson: Speak the truth to family even when it costs you; leave if you must, without hatred.

verse.for_you: You are not less for speaking the truth and leaving. A quiet flat is not the end of your worth. The door you close is the one that was already shut to you.
verse.try_today: Notice one thing today that is still yours alone, without asking for permission.

why: walking away with dignity after counsel is refused
no curse, only a blessing at the door

story.title: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
story.story_hook: She came to him with her hair still unbound, thirteen years of humiliation in her voice.
story.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
story.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.
story.hook_title: Draupadi came to Krishna with her hair still unbound after thirteen years
story.teaser: Draupadi came to Krishna with her hair still unbound after thirteen years

verse.speaker: Draupadi
verse.setting: Before Krishna's peace mission, Draupadi recalls the dice-hall, where her husbands sat silent.
verse.sanskrit: निरमर्षेष्वचेष्टेषु प्रेक्ष्यमाणेषु पाण्डुषु / पाहि मामिति गोविन्द मनसा चिन्तितोसि मे
verse.line: When those who should have protected me only watched, I called to you in my heart: protect me.
verse.translation: While the sons of Pandu sat without anger or movement, only watching, I thought of you in my mind, Govinda: 'Protect me!'
verse.why: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.
verse.misuse: Draupadi's inner prayer did not replace speaking up: she also challenged the whole court. Prayer is not a reason to stay silent about abuse.

prasang.title: Draupadi tells Krishna her sorrow
prasang.summary: Krishna visits the exiled Pandavas in the Kamyaka forest and tells Arjuna 'you are mine and I am yours'. Draupadi then comes to him 'seeking refuge with the refuge', tells him, out of closeness, everything done to her in the dice-hall and since, and weeps that she has no one, not even him. Krishna promises she will see justice.
prasang.story_hook: She came to him with her hair still unbound, thirteen years of humiliation in her voice.
prasang.lesson: You can bring God your rawest pain, even your sense of being abandoned, and be heard.

verse.for_you: You are not wrong to feel the silence of the flat. You called out in your heart because the watching was too much to bear alone. Your grief is a just thing, and you do not have to hold it by yourself.
verse.try_today: Notice one moment today when you call out for protection, and let it be a real call.
verse.scene_line: You stand in the quiet flat, and you call to the one who has always been your refuge.

why: Alone in a full hall
The people who should have protected me only watched. Who do I have?

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse.sanskrit: अवलेपः समुद्रस्य न दर्शयति यः स्वयम्। प्रशमश्च क्षमा चैव आर्जवं प्रियवादिता॥ असामर्थ्यफला ह्येते निर्गुणेषु सतां गुणाः।
verse.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.
verse.why: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
verse.misuse: Firmness only after real patience, and only toward someone who keeps ignoring you. When the ocean finally came, Ram listened and redirected the arrow.

prasang.title: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasang.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasang.story_hook: For three days the prince lay on a bed of grass at the edge of the sea, asking politely.
prasang.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.

why: patience was offered and treated as incapacity
Humble first, firm after (Valmiki Ramayana, Yuddha Kanda 21-22)

verse.speaker: Sita
verse.setting: Alone in captivity, Sita fears Ram has forgotten her, then reassures herself.
verse.sanskrit: दृश्यमाने भवेत् प्रीतिः सौहृदं नास्त्यदृश्यतः। नाशयन्ति कृतघ्नास्तु न रामो नाशयिष्यति॥
verse.line: 'Out of sight, out of mind' is true only of the ungrateful. Real love survives distance.
verse.translation: Love lasts while someone is in sight; out of sight, affection fades. But that is the way of the ungrateful. Ram will not let it fade.
verse.why: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.

prasang.title: Sita in captivity
prasang.summary: Guards threaten Sita day and night. She fears Ram has forgotten her, then reminds herself that out of sight is out of mind only for the ungrateful. The guard Trijata dreams of Ram's victory, and good omens begin to appear.
prasang.story_hook: She had been alone in the grove for ten months, surrounded by guards who mocked her every day.
prasang.lesson: Hold on to love across distance; hope can arrive from unexpected people.

verse.for_you: You are not less than you were. The silence in your flat does not mean you have been forgotten. Hold to what you know of your own worth.
verse.try_today: Notice one small thing that shows you are still seen and valued.
verse.scene_line: Sita stands alone in the Ashoka grove, and you stand alone in the quiet flat, both holding to what you know of love.

why: Remembering is a kind of nearness.
she answers the fear from what she knows of him

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse.sanskrit: ब्रह्मण्याधाय कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा करोति यः । लिप्यते न स पापेन पद्मपत्रमिवाम्भसा ॥
verse.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.
verse.why: Be in the mess without letting it soak in.
verse.misuse: Staying unstained isn't staying silent about wrongdoing at work; you can act and still keep your peace.

prasang.title: Marks of the knower and the doer
prasang.summary: The disciplined person acts without attachment, like a lotus leaf untouched by water, and finds peace by letting go of the fruit.
prasang.lesson: Be in the mess without letting it soak in.

why: Like a lotus leaf in water.
the claim on one's work is given away, so the work stops clinging
plan_v3.writer_note: Letting-go teaching for a reader who is young and afraid of being left. Explain it through their own situation and feeling: what is released is the grip that hurts them, never their love, their hope or their work. Never say or imply 'stop caring' or 'your hope is the problem'. Read it after the guard verse, which reassures first.

guard.line: 'Out of sight, out of mind' is true only of the ungrateful. Real love survives distance.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse.sanskrit: चेतसा सर्वकर्माणि मयि संन्यस्य मत्परः । बुद्धियोगमुपाश्रित्य मच्चित्तः सततं भव ॥
verse.line: Inwardly hand all your work to the divine, hold it as your goal, and keep your mind on it.
verse.translation: Mentally resigning all actions to me, holding me as the highest, relying on the yoga of understanding, keep your mind always on me.
verse.why: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

prasang.title: Action with devotion: surrender
prasang.summary: Krishna urges Arjuna to offer all action, warns that ego will only trip him, tells him to reflect fully and then choose, and finally to take refuge in him alone and not grieve.
prasang.lesson: Reflect fully, choose freely, and set down the fear.

verse.for_you: The flat is quiet now, and the weight of the last twelve years feels like it belongs to no one but you. Hand it over. Hold the divine as your highest goal. Keep your mind on that, and let it carry you through the silence.
verse.try_today: Resign your work and grief to the divine, and hold the divine as your highest goal.
verse.scene_line: Like Arjuna on the battlefield, you stand before a great loss and must offer your work to the divine alone.

why: him as the highest goal
Hand the work over, drop 'mine'.

verse.speaker: Tulsidas
verse.setting: Angad walks alone into Ravana's hostile court as Ram's envoy.
verse.sanskrit: गयउ सभा दरबार तब सुमिरि राम पद कंज। सिंह ठवनि इत उत चितव धीर बीर बल पुंज ॥
verse.line: He walked into the hostile room remembering Ram, steady as a lion.
verse.translation: Then he went into the court, remembering Ram's lotus feet, looking this way and that with a lion's gait, steady, brave, a mass of strength.

why: he looks around the court without shrinking
he goes in remembering Ram's feet

story.title: Nala and Damayanti
story.story_hook: The more King Nala lost at dice, the less he could stop.
story.summary: King Nala, possessed by the spirit Kali, gambles away his kingdom to his brother and abandons Damayanti in the forest. Years of separation and disguise follow, until Nala masters the dice and the two are reunited.
story.lesson: Compulsions can take everything. Loyalty and patience can still bring you home.
story.hook_title: The more King Nala lost at dice, the less he could stop
story.teaser: The more King Nala lost at dice, the less he could stop

why: Even in total loss a person can grieve fully and still decide what she will and will not accept.

queries.act: Reach out to the people and the practice that hold you; seek good company, and remember you are never truly alone.
queries.story: A story of a student who came to a teacher with questions and was led, step by step, toward the truth.

understanding.life_context: Working. Feels searching; closest to "I want to reconnect with my roots" and "I don't know my purpose".

verse.speaker: Bharat
verse.setting: Bharat, urged by his teacher and mother to accept the throne, explains why he cannot.
verse.sanskrit: तुम्ह तौ देहु सरल सिख सोई। जो आचरत मोर भल होई॥ जद्यपि यह समुझत हउँ नीकें। तदपि होत परितोष न जी कें ॥
verse.line: I understand your advice perfectly. My heart still isn't at peace.
verse.translation: You give me simple advice, the kind that would do me good if I followed it. Though I understand it well, my heart is not at peace.
verse.why: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

prasang.title: Bharat refuses the throne
prasang.summary: After the funeral, Vasishtha, the ministers and Kausalya all urge Bharat to rule, as his father wished. Bharat says the advice is right and his heart still isn't at peace; the crown means nothing without Ram. He decides to go to the forest, admit his fault, and trust his brother to forgive.
prasang.story_hook: Everyone agreed the throne was his, and Bharat could not bring himself to sit on it.
prasang.lesson: When head and heart disagree, go and face the person you think you wronged.

verse.for_you: Understanding the right step does not settle the heart. Your mind sees the quiet, but your grief still fills the room.
verse.try_today: Notice one sound the quiet makes today.
verse.scene_line: Bharat understands the crown is right, but his heart still seeks Ram, and so you seek Bruno.

why: understanding does not reach the grief

verse.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse.sanskrit: न श्रेयः सततं तेजो न नित्यं श्रेयसी क्षमा / इति तात विजानीहि द्वयमेतदसंशयम्
verse.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.
verse.why: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.
verse.misuse: Forgiveness never means accepting ongoing harm; this verse itself says it has limits.

prasang.title: Forgiveness or force: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
prasang.summary: In the forest, Draupadi asks why Yudhishthira does not answer injustice with anger, citing Prahlada's advice that neither force nor forgiveness is always right. Yudhishthira replies that anger destroys and forgiveness holds the world together.
prasang.story_hook: Thirteen years into exile, Draupadi looked at her husband and asked why he was not angry.
prasang.lesson: Anger rarely heals anything; forgiveness has limits. Wisdom is knowing which a moment needs.

plan_v3.path: mbh.3.28.6 [whose smallness it is: curated list for the wronged stance]
why: Not always force, not always forgiveness: the question of how to respond is a real one.

verse.speaker: Krishna
verse.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse.sanskrit: यो मां पश्यति सर्वत्र सर्वं च मयि पश्यति । तस्याहं न प्रणश्यामि स च मे न प्रणश्यति ॥
verse.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.
verse.why: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

prasang.title: Meditation in detail
prasang.summary: Krishna describes meditation: moderation in food and sleep, the mind like a lamp in a windless place, bringing the wandering mind back, and feeling others' joy and pain as one's own.
prasang.lesson: Moderation and gentle return, again and again, settle the mind.

why: Never lost to me.
'I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me': the bond cannot be broken by distance

verse.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse.setting: Lecture 'Work and Its Secret', Los Angeles, 4 January 1900. On those who avoid pain by never loving.
verse.line: the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
verse.translation: Therefore the man who never loves, who is hard and stony, escaping most of the miseries of life, escapes also its joys.
verse.why: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

prasang.title: Work and its secret (Los Angeles, 1900)
prasang.summary: His greatest lesson, he says, was to attend to the means as much as the end. Most failures come from neglecting the means, and most sorrow from clinging to what is already failing. Weakness invites misery, yet a heart that refuses to love also loses life's joys.
prasang.lesson: Look after the means; keep the power to let go.

verse.try_today: Notice one small thing today that still carries the shape of your love.
verse.scene_line: You are not the man who never loves, and that is why the silence hurts.

why: the urge to shut down is answered
the pain is the other side of having loved, and the alternative was stone

verse.speaker: The gods
verse.setting: The gods' hymn to the Goddess, a verse shared with the Vedic Durga Suktam.
verse.sanskrit: तामग्निवर्णां तपसा ज्वलन्तीं वैरोचनीं कर्मफलेषु जुष्टाम् । दुर्गां देवीं शरणमहं प्रपद्ये सुतरां नाशयते तमः ॥
verse.line: I take refuge in Durga, the blazing Goddess. She clears away the darkness.
verse.translation: She who is fire-coloured, blazing with austerity, radiant, sought by those who act: in Durga, the Goddess, I take refuge. She utterly destroys the darkness.
verse.why: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.
verse.misuse: Refuge in the Goddess is strength to face hardship, not a guarantee it will vanish.

prasang.title: The gods ask the Goddess: who are you?
prasang.summary: All the gods come to the Goddess and ask who she is. She answers that she is the highest reality, the source of nature and spirit. The gods bow, praise her as the Mother who protects on every side, and take refuge in her as Durga, who carries beings through hard places.
prasang.story_hook: Even the gods did not know who she was, so one day they simply went and asked her.
prasang.lesson: The Mother who is everything is also near enough to be called on in fear.

verse.try_today: Notice one small thing that still burns with life today.
verse.scene_line: You sit in the quiet flat, and the blazing Goddess clears away the darkness around you.

why: the refuge is fierce, and lends that fierceness
'I take refuge'

verse.speaker: Ram
verse.setting: After three days of patient requests, Ram turns to Lakshman.
verse.sanskrit: क्षमया हि समायुक्तं मामयं मकरालयः॥ असमर्थ विजानाति धिक्क्षमामीदृशे जने। न दर्शयति साम्ना मे सागरो रूपमात्मनः॥ चापमानय सौमित्रे शरांश्चाशीविषोपमान्। समुद्रं शोषयिष्यामि पद्भयां यान्तु प्लवंगमाः॥
verse.line: My patience was taken for weakness. Gentle asking didn't work. Lakshman, bring my bow.
verse.translation: Because I am forbearing, this ocean takes me to be incapable. Shame on forbearance toward such a one. Gentle means have not made him show himself. Lakshman, bring my bow and arrows.
verse.why: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.
verse.misuse: Firmness only after real patience, and only toward someone who keeps ignoring you. When the ocean finally came, Ram listened and redirected the arrow.

prasang.title: Ram at the ocean: humble first, firm after
prasang.summary: Ram lies on kusha grass by the shore for three days, asking the ocean for a way. Ignored, he tells Lakshman that patience is being taken for weakness and takes up his bow. The ocean rises, offers a way (Nala's bridge), and Ram releases the arrow elsewhere at its request.
prasang.story_hook: For three days the prince lay on a bed of grass at the edge of the sea, asking politely.
prasang.lesson: Be humble first. When humility is taken for weakness, act firmly, and stop once you're heard.

verse.try_today: Notice the moment you stop bending and stand firm.
verse.scene_line: You stand at the shore, having asked the quiet for a way, and now you ask for a bow.

why: firmness taken up only after gentleness was tried in full
Humble first, firm after

story.title: Kunti watches her sons and daughter-in-law walk into exile
story.story_hook: She was too old to go with them. She stood at the gate and said one thing to her daughter-in-law, and then she wept.
story.summary: Kunti is too old for the forest, so Vidura will keep her in his house. She watches her five sons leave in deerskins, heads down, mocked by Duhshasana. Draupadi comes to take her leave in a single stained garment with her hair loose.
story.lesson: A parent's part, when the children must go, is to bless them truthfully and bear the waiting.
story.teaser: She was too old to go with them. She stood at the gate and said one thing to her daughter-in-law, and then she wept.

why: A parent's part, when the children must go, is to bless them truthfully and bear the waiting.
